title: Small Bowel Obstruction
scenario: A 62-year-old male with a prior open appendectomy presents to the emergency department with 2 days of crampy abdominal pain, abdominal distension, and vomiting. He has not passed stool or flatus since yesterday.

lines: 62-year-old male reports 2 days of intermittent crampy periumbilical pain, progressive abdominal distension, and multiple episodes of bilious vomiting. No stool or flatus since the previous day. History of open appendectomy 15 years ago. Abdomen distended and tympanic; high-pitched, tinkling bowel sounds early, now hypoactive. Reports nausea. Mucous membranes dry. Alert and oriented x3.
IV access obtained. Labs, upright and supine abdominal x-ray, and CT abdomen ordered. NPO status maintained. Cardiac monitor applied.
Nasogastric tube inserted to low intermittent suction per order, draining bilious fluid. IV isotonic fluids started. Foley catheter inserted to monitor output.
Reports abdominal pain and nausea decreased. Abdomen softer, less distended. NG tube draining freely. Passed a small amount of flatus. Voided 250 mL clear yellow urine since fluids started.
Insert nasogastric tube to low intermittent suction
Insert indwelling urinary catheter, strict intake and output
IV potassium chloride 20 mEq per protocol for potassium 3.2
Notify provider for fever, worsening pain, or urine output < 30 mL/hr

children.subject: Medical-Surgical
children.stem: Which 4 findings are consistent with a small bowel obstruction and require follow-up?

options.text: No passage of stool or flatus

children.rationale: Bilious vomiting, distension with tympany, obstipation, and early high-pitched bowel sounds are classic cues of mechanical small bowel obstruction. Normal orientation and oxygenation are expected findings.

children.subject: Medical-Surgical
children.stem: For each finding, click to specify whether it indicates fluid volume deficit, an electrolyte imbalance, or both. Each finding may support more than one.
children.rationale: An elevated BUN/creatinine ratio, tachycardia, and dry membranes reflect dehydration from vomiting and third-spacing. Loss of gastric fluid depletes potassium and chloride, producing electrolyte imbalance.

children.subject: Medical-Surgical
children.stem: Complete the sentence. The nurse determines that the priority problem for this client is {1}, and the earliest sign of the feared complication would be {2}.

choices.text: deficient fluid volume from vomiting and bowel sequestration
worsening pain with fever and rising lactate

children.rationale: Fluid and electrolyte loss is the most immediate life threat and takes priority. Bowel strangulation and ischemia are the feared complication; escalating pain, fever, and a rising lactate are its earliest warning signs.

children.subject: Medical-Surgical
children.stem: For each intervention, click to specify whether it is indicated or contraindicated for this client.

rows.text: Insert a nasogastric tube to low intermittent suction
Give a stimulant laxative to promote a bowel movement
Offer clear liquids by mouth to relieve thirst

children.rationale: NPO, gastric decompression, IV fluid resuscitation, and potassium replacement manage a bowel obstruction. Laxatives and oral intake are contraindicated because they increase intraluminal contents and worsen distension or vomiting.

children.subject: Medical-Surgical
children.stem: After inserting the nasogastric tube to suction and starting IV fluids, which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Verify nasogastric tube placement and confirm suction is functioning
Measure and document strict intake and output
Monitor serum potassium and other electrolytes
Irrigate the nasogastric tube with tap water every hour routinely
Advance the client to a full diet once nausea improves

children.rationale: The nurse confirms tube placement and patency, tracks fluid balance, and monitors electrolytes lost through gastric drainage. Routine hourly tap-water irrigation and diet advancement are not indicated while the obstruction is unresolved.

children.subject: Medical-Surgical
children.stem: Which findings indicate the treatment has been effective? Select all that apply.

options.text: Urine output of 250 mL after fluids

children.rationale: Return of flatus, reduced distension, normalizing vital signs, and adequate urine output all show the obstruction and fluid deficit are resolving. Increasing vomiting would indicate the obstruction is worsening.
